summaryTr: Gezgin satıcı Gregor Samsa bir sabah uyandığında korkunç bir yaratığa dönüştüğünü fark eder. Kafka'nın ünlü öyküsünün, ailesinin bu açıklanamayan olay karşısında nasıl değiştiğini anlatan kısaltılmış İngilizce uyarlaması.
paragraphs: ## I. The Morning

Waking one morning out of a night of unquiet dreams, Gregor Samsa discovered that, there in his bed, he had become an immense and repulsive vermin. The back he was lying on was hard as armour plating. By raising his head a fraction he could see the brown vault of his belly, ribbed with stiff arching bands, the quilt perched on its summit and about to slide off. His legs – a great many of them, and wretchedly thin for a body of that bulk – flickered uselessly in front of his eyes.

“What has become of me?” he thought. This was no dream. Around him, quiet within walls he knew by heart, stood his room – an ordinary room for a human being, only somewhat on the small side. His cloth samples lay unpacked across the table, for Samsa travelled for a living, and above them hung a picture he had clipped from an illustrated magazine and given a pretty gilt frame. In it a lady sat bolt upright in a fur hat and a fur stole, offering to the viewer a weighty muff that had swallowed her entire forearm.

Rain was striking the metal sill outside. Suppose he slept on a little and forgot all this foolishness? It could not be done: however hard he flung himself to the right, his usual sleeping side, he swung back like a rocking toy. “Good God, what a wearing trade I picked!” he thought. “Travelling, day in, day out; the worry about connections, miserable meals at all hours, acquaintances that never grow into anything warmer!” Were it not for his parents, he would have handed in his notice long ago. Once he had put by enough to clear their debt to his employer – five or six years more, perhaps – he would make a clean cut. For now, though, he had to get up. His train was at five.

His eyes went to the clock on the chest, ticking away. Heavens – half past six already, the hands calmly moving on. Could the alarm have failed to ring? There was a train at seven, but the firm’s errand boy would have reported him long ago. Should he call in sick? Gregor had not been ill once in all his years with the firm, and the health-insurance doctor held that the world was populated entirely by healthy people who shirked work. Nor, in truth, did Gregor feel unwell, apart from a pointless drowsiness. If anything, he was ravenous.

A careful knock came at the door beside the head of his bed. “Gregor, dear,” called his mother, “it’s a quarter to seven. Shouldn’t you be on your way?” His own answer startled him. It was unmistakably his old voice, but beneath it, as if from somewhere lower down, ran a thin, painful piping that let each word ring clearly for an instant and then smeared it. “Yes, yes, thank you, Mother – I’ll be up in a moment,” was all he risked, and the wooden door seemed to hide the change. Yet now the whole family knew he had not left. At one side door his father was knocking, feebly but with his fist; at the other his sister asked in a low voice, “Gregor? Are you not well? Can I get you anything?” To both he answered, “Nearly ready,” shaping every syllable with care. Then his sister whispered: “Gregor, please, I implore you – open up.” He had no such intention, and blessed instead the habit, learned in hotels, of locking every door overnight, even at home.
## The Chief Clerk

The altered voice, Gregor was certain, meant nothing worse than a heavy chill on its way, the travelling man’s occupational complaint. The quilt was easy: he puffed himself out and it slid off. After that everything grew hard. He would have needed arms and hands to raise himself; instead he had dozens of little legs, all in ceaseless motion and none under his command. At last he began rocking his whole length out over the edge of the bed.

He already jutted halfway out when the bell of the flat rang. The visitor’s first word of greeting told him who it was – none other than the chief clerk. Driven more by agitation than by any real resolve, Gregor heaved himself out with all his might and hit the floor with a muffled thud.

“Something has fallen in there,” remarked the chief clerk next door, to the left. Then came the father’s voice: “Gregor, the gentleman from the firm is asking why you weren’t on the early train. Open the door, please.” “He’s not well, sir, believe me,” the mother put in. “The boy has nothing in his head but business. The most he allows himself is a little fretwork – he carved a small frame, you’ll be astonished how pretty it is.” “So may the gentleman come in to you now?” asked the father, losing patience. “No,” said Gregor. On the left an embarrassed hush followed; on the right, his sister broke into sobs.

The chief clerk now spoke more loudly. “Mr Samsa, what is the meaning of this? You barricade yourself in, you cause your parents needless anxiety, and you neglect your duties to the firm in a manner that is, frankly, beyond belief. Early today the head of the firm hinted at a reason for your absence – the cash collections lately placed in your hands – and I very nearly staked my honour on its being untrue. Your standing is far from firm. Granted, this is not the season for remarkable sales. But a season for no sales whatever does not exist, Mr Samsa. It cannot be allowed to exist.”

“But sir!” Gregor cried, frantic. “I’m opening it this very moment! A fit of giddiness kept me lying here, but I’m fresh again now. Don’t blame my parents! I’ll be on the eight o’clock train, and my compliments to the head of the firm!” While these words tumbled out of him, he crept across to the chest, slid off its smooth side several times, and at last hauled himself upright against it.

“Did either of you follow a single word?” the clerk asked the parents. “Oh God,” wept the mother, “he may be gravely ill! Grete, the doctor – quickly!” “That,” said the clerk, conspicuously quiet beside her cries, “was an animal’s voice.” “Anna!” shouted the father towards the kitchen, clapping his hands. “A locksmith, this instant!” Skirts rustling, the two girls ran out, leaving the front door open, as it tends to be left in homes that some great calamity has struck.

Gregor, for his part, had grown much calmer. His words could no longer be made out, but at least everyone now accepted that something was amiss and stood ready to help. Once more he felt part of the company of human beings. He shoved a chair over, propped himself upright against the door – the pads at the ends of his legs were faintly sticky – and began to work the key round with his mouth. Real teeth he seemed to lack, but his jaws were strong, even if a brown juice ran down the key onto the floor. “Just listen,” said the clerk beyond the wall, “the key is turning.” Gregor clamped onto it with all his strength until the bolt sprang back with a brighter click. “So the locksmith was not needed,” he told himself.
## Through the Door

Opened this way, the door stood wide before any part of Gregor came into view, and he still had to edge carefully round its one wing. He was busy with this when a loud “Oh!” burst from the chief clerk, like a gust of wind, and Gregor saw him clap a hand to his gaping mouth and give ground little by little, as if some unseen pressure were driving him off. The mother, her hair still undone from the night, came two steps towards her son and collapsed among her billowing skirts, her face sunk on her breast. The father made a fist, his look hostile, as though he meant to knock Gregor back inside; then he put both hands over his eyes and sobbed, his powerful chest heaving.

“Well, then,” said Gregor, conscious that he alone had kept his composure, “I’ll dress straight away, pack up the samples and be off. You see, sir, I’m not pig-headed, and I enjoy the work. I’m in a tight spot just now, but I’ll get clear of it again. Only, at the office, please take my side!” At Gregor’s very first words, however, the clerk had turned away, and now, never once letting him out of his sight, he was sidling towards the hall. There he stretched one arm far out towards the staircase, as if a positively heavenly deliverance awaited him on the landing.

The man could not be allowed to leave in this frame of mind, or Gregor’s post was finished. He released his hold on the door, squeezed through the gap and came down with a small cry onto all his little legs. At once, for the first time since waking, he felt a kind of bodily ease: the floor was solid beneath him, and the legs did exactly as he wished. All his suffering, he believed, was about to be cured.

At that instant his mother leapt up, arms thrown wide. “Help, for the love of God, help!” she cried, and, running senselessly backwards, sat down in a rush on the laid table without noticing that the big pot had tipped over and coffee was gushing onto the rug. “Mother, Mother,” Gregor murmured, and seeing the coffee stream out he could not keep his jaws from snapping several times at nothing. That set her screaming again; she ran from the table into the father’s arms.

The chief clerk, meanwhile, had reached the stairs. Gregor made a dash after him, but the man cleared several steps in a single bound and was gone, his cry of “Huh!” ringing through the stairwell. This flight threw the father into complete confusion. Snatching up the stick the visitor had left on a chair, and a big newspaper in his other hand, he began, stamping and making savage hissing sounds, to drive Gregor back towards his room. Gregor begged in vain; nobody understood him. When at last he had turned round, his body proved too broad for the half-open doorway, and opening the second wing never crossed the father’s mind. Come what may, Gregor forced himself into the gap and jammed there, one flank scraped raw, ugly smears left on the white paint – until a hard shove from behind, a real deliverance, sent him flying, blood streaming, to the far side of the room. A blow of the stick banged the door to. Then there was silence at last.
## II. A Sister’s Care

Only at dusk did Gregor come out of a heavy sleep close to a faint. One leg, badly hurt that morning, trailed lifeless behind him, and his left side seemed a single long scar that pulled unpleasantly. By the door stood a bowl of sweetened milk with sops of white bread swimming in it. Milk had always been his favourite drink, which was surely why his sister had put it there; yet now it tasted of nothing he wanted, and he turned away almost in revulsion. At night the high, bare room alarmed him, and half ashamed he scuttled beneath the sofa, where he felt snug at once. For now, he concluded, he had to keep still and, with patience and the utmost tact, make his condition as little of a burden to his family as he could.

At first light his sister, already almost dressed, looked in from the hall. Catching sight of him under the sofa, she was so frightened that she slammed the door; then, as though sorry, she opened it again and tiptoed in, the way one might enter the room of a stranger. Seeing the milk untouched, she came back, in her goodness, with a whole assortment on old newspaper to learn what he liked: vegetables half gone bad, bones in a sauce that had set firm, some almonds and raisins, a cheese Gregor had called uneatable two days earlier, and some bread. Knowing he would never eat with her watching, she hurried out. Eyes wet with contentment, he gobbled up the cheese, then the vegetables and sauce; fresh food he could not even bear to smell.

This became the routine: twice each day his sister brought him food. As he could not be understood, it occurred to no one, not even to her, that he might understand them. “Today he enjoyed it,” she would say; or, more and more often, in an almost mournful tone: “Everything’s been left again.” Pressed flat against his door, he picked up other news. The maid had begged on her knees, that very first day, to be let go. And his father, whose business had failed five years before, had after all kept a little money from those days; part of Gregor’s monthly earnings had been put aside too. Gregor nodded eagerly, pleased at such unlooked-for thrift. The money could have paid off more of the debt and freed him from the job sooner; but no doubt his father’s arrangement was wiser.

After that failure Gregor had worked with a special fire, putting his commission down in cash before his astonished, delighted family. Splendid times, never repeated with the same glow; the family grew used to the money, and no particular warmth came of it. Only his sister had stayed close. She loved music and could play the violin so as to move a listener, and Gregor’s secret plan was that next year, whatever the expense, she should study at the conservatory. He had meant to announce it, solemnly, on Christmas Eve.

Yet the savings would last one year, two at the outside. His father was old and had grown fat; his mother suffered from asthma; his sister was a child of seventeen. Whenever the talk came round to earning money, Gregor flung himself down on the cool leather of the sofa, hot with shame and sorrow. Some nights he shoved the armchair to the window and leaned on the sill, though each day he saw less, until he might have been looking out on a desert where grey sky and grey earth ran together without a seam.

His sister still found the sight of him unbearable. On coming in she would hurry straight to the window, as if she were stifling, and fling it open. To spare her, Gregor one day hauled a sheet onto the sofa on his back – the work took him four hours – and draped it so that nothing of him showed. She left it as it was, and once, when he raised a corner with his head, he thought he caught a look of gratitude.
## The Empty Room

For distraction Gregor took to crawling over walls and ceiling. He liked best to hang up there; one breathed more freely, and in that almost happy absorption he sometimes let go and smacked onto the floor, yet came to no harm. His sister noticed the sticky traces he left and decided to give him more room by clearing out the furniture, above all the chest and the desk. She could not manage alone, so one day, while the father was out, she brought the mother.

Gregor drew the sheet lower and heard the two frail women shoving the heavy old chest. After a long while the mother whispered: “Isn’t it as if, by taking his things away, we were telling him we have no hope left? Surely it is best to keep the room just as it was, so that when Gregor returns to us he will find nothing altered and can forget this whole time more easily.”

Listening to her, Gregor realised that two months without a single word addressed straight to him must have muddled his thinking. Did he really wish to see his warm room, so comfortably furnished with inherited pieces, made into a cave where he might crawl freely in all directions – while rapidly forgetting his human past? He was near to forgetting already. Nothing must be taken out. All of it had to remain.

But Grete had grown used to playing the expert in all that concerned Gregor, and her mother’s advice only made her insist that everything go except the sofa. Perhaps, too, a girlish romantic streak tempted her to make his plight more frightening still, so as to be all the more indispensable. For a room in which Gregor reigned alone over bare walls was a room no one but Grete would ever venture into.

Out went the chest, then, with the fretsaw and the rest of his tools in it, and now they were loosening the desk at which he had written his lessons since he was a small boy. That was more than he could bear. He burst out from under the sofa, changed course four times, unsure what to rescue first, and then, on a wall already stripped, his eye fell on the lady clad in furs. He scrambled up and pressed himself to the glass, soothing to his feverish belly. This picture, at any rate, nobody would carry off.

The women came back, and Grete’s gaze met Gregor’s on the wall. Trembling, she tried to steer her mother out again, but the mother stepped aside, saw the huge brown blot on the flowered wallpaper and, before she had grasped that it was Gregor, cried out hoarsely, “Oh God, oh God!” and dropped across the sofa with arms flung wide. “You – Gregor!” cried his sister, shaking her fist at him – the first words she had addressed to him since the transformation. She ran next door for some essence to bring her mother round. Gregor tore himself from the glass and followed, as though he could advise her as in former days; she spun round, startled, a bottle smashed on the floor, and a splinter cut his face. Grete rushed back to her mother with an armful of bottles and kicked the door shut. Shut out, racked by self-reproach, Gregor crawled over walls, furniture and ceiling alike, until the whole room was turning round him and he fell onto the middle of the big table.
## The Apples

The bell rang; the father had come home. “Mother fainted, but she’s recovering,” said Grete, her face against his chest. “Gregor has broken out.” “Just what I expected,” said the father. “I always told you so, but you women won’t listen.” Gregor saw that his father imagined some act of violence, so he hurried to his own door and flattened himself against it, to show that he wanted nothing but to go back in.

“Ah!” the father cried the instant he entered, sounding at once enraged and pleased. Gregor lifted his head towards him. Was this still his father – the man who had lain sunk wearily in bed when Gregor set out on his trips, and who on their rare Sunday walks had toiled along on his crutch-handled stick? Now he stood fully erect, buttoned into a close-fitting blue uniform with gilt buttons, such as the messengers of banks wear; his white hair was combed into a painfully exact, gleaming parting. He sent his cap sailing over to the sofa and came at Gregor with a set, grim face. He raised his feet strangely high, and Gregor marvelled at the gigantic soles of his boots.

So Gregor ran ahead of him, halting whenever the father halted and scurrying on again the moment he stirred. They circled the room like this more than once, so slowly that it hardly looked like a chase; yet Gregor was soon short of breath. Then something sailed down close beside him and rolled on ahead: an apple. A second came straight after it. The father had filled his pockets from the fruit dish on the sideboard and was now pelting him, apple after apple. The small red apples rolled about the floor as if charged with electricity. One weak throw only brushed Gregor’s back and glanced off; the very next one sank right into it. Gregor tried to crawl onward, as though the astonishing pain might be left behind, but he felt pinned where he was. With his last look he saw his mother hurry out in her chemise, her loosened skirts slipping to the floor one after another, stumble to his father, embrace him and, with her hands at the back of his head, plead for Gregor’s life.
## III. Evenings with the Door Open

Nobody dared to take the apple out, so it stayed embedded in Gregor’s flesh as a visible reminder, and the wound plagued him for over a month. It seemed to have brought home even to the father that, however loathsome his shape, Gregor belonged to the family; family duty demanded that they choke down their revulsion and endure – endure and nothing else. Like some aged invalid, he now needed long minutes to cross his room; climbing seemed out of the question. In return, every evening the living-room door was opened, and from the dark of his room, unseen, he could watch the whole family round the lamplit table.

These were not the lively talks he used to long for in narrow hotel rooms. Soon after supper the father fell asleep in his armchair, still in the uniform he refused to take off even at home; the mother bent over fine linen she sewed for a fashion shop; the sister, now a salesgirl, learned shorthand and French at night. At ten it took the two women fifteen minutes of coaxing to get the father to bed. “So this is my life,” he would say. “This is my peaceful old age.”

Who in this worn-out family had time for Gregor beyond the bare necessities? The maid was dismissed after all; a huge, bony charwoman with fluttering white hair came mornings and evenings for the heaviest chores. Family jewellery was sold. The flat, too big now, could not be given up, they lamented, because of Gregor. Yet he could easily have been shipped in a box with some holes for air; what held them back was sheer hopelessness, the sense that misfortune had singled them out as it had no one else they knew.

His sister had stopped asking what might please him. Before work she nudged whatever food was at hand in at his door with her foot, and in the evening a flick of the broom swept it out again, mostly untasted. Dirt streaked the walls; knots of dust lay in the corners. Yet when the mother once scrubbed the room, Grete, mortally offended, burst into tears, the father railed at both women, and Gregor hissed with rage that nobody thought of shutting the door.

The charwoman, a sturdy old widow, felt no real horror of him. She would open his door a crack and call to him in words she presumably considered friendly: “Come on over here, old dung beetle!” One early morning, while heavy rain – perhaps already a herald of spring – lashed the panes, Gregor turned on her as if to attack, though slowly and feebly. Unafraid, she simply raised a chair high in the air, her mouth hanging wide open. “So – that’s as far as it goes?” she asked when he turned back, and calmly returned the chair to its corner.
## The Violin

Gregor hardly ate at all now. One of the rooms had been let to three lodgers, serious gentlemen, all with full beards, who were sticklers for order throughout the household, the kitchen above all. Whatever could not be stored elsewhere – superfluous furniture, the ash bin, the rubbish bin – landed in Gregor’s room. He wound his way through the clutter, later with growing pleasure, though after such outings he lay motionless for hours, deathly tired and miserable.

One evening the charwoman had not quite shut the living-room door. The lodgers sat at the top of the table, where once the father, the mother and Gregor had sat, and the women carried in steaming meat and potatoes; the family itself ate in the kitchen. Out of all the noises of the meal Gregor kept hearing their chewing teeth, as though to prove to him that teeth were needed for eating. “I do have an appetite,” he told himself sorrowfully, “only not for these things. How these lodgers stuff themselves, while I perish!”

That same evening, from the kitchen, came the sound of the violin. The middle gentleman asked whether the young lady would not rather play in here, where it was much more comfortable. “Oh, by all means,” cried the father, as though he himself were the performer. The parents, who had never let rooms before and overdid their courtesy towards the lodgers, did not dare to take their own chairs.

The sister started to play. Gregor, drawn by the music, crept forward until his head was over the threshold of the living room. Dusty all over, trailing threads, hairs and scraps of food on his back, he felt no shyness about advancing across the immaculate floor. Nobody paid him any heed. The lodgers soon retreated to the window, heads lowered, muttering; they plainly felt let down and put up with the music only out of courtesy. And how beautifully she played! Head tilted, she followed the lines of notes with probing, sorrowful eyes. Could he be an animal, if music seized him so? It was as though the road to the unknown food he yearned for were opening before him. He would go right up to her and pluck at her skirt, to hint that she should bring her violin into his room, since nobody here honoured her playing as he would. He would never let her leave again; for the first time his terrifying shape would be of some use. He would confide to her that he had firmly intended her to go to the conservatory; she would weep, deeply moved, and he would raise himself as high as her shoulder and kiss the bare neck.

“Mr Samsa!” cried the middle gentleman, pointing a forefinger at Gregor. The violin fell silent. The father rushed to herd the lodgers back into their room, and that did make them angry. At their door the middle gentleman stamped. “I hereby give notice,” he declared, “that in view of the revolting conditions in this flat and this family” – here he spat on the floor – “I am leaving my room this instant. Naturally I shall pay nothing whatsoever for the days I have spent here, and I may well bring claims against you.” His two friends chimed in at once: “We, too, give notice, this instant.” The door shut with a crash.
## It Has to Go

The father tottered to his armchair and sank into it. Gregor still lay on the spot where the lodgers had caught him, too disappointed and too weak with hunger to stir. Not even the violin startled him when it slid from his mother’s trembling fingers and gave out a resounding note.

“Dear parents,” said his sister, bringing her hand down on the table, “it cannot go on like this. I will not speak my brother’s name in front of this creature, so all I say is this: we must somehow get rid of it. To nurse it and put up with it, we have done all that people can do. I don’t believe anyone could reproach us in the slightest.”

“She is right a thousand times over,” said the father, half to himself. The mother began coughing hollowly into her hand. “It’s going to kill you both; I see it coming,” Grete went on, in tears. “When all of us must slave the way we do, we cannot bear this eternal torture at home on top of it. I can’t, not any more.”
“My child,” said the father, “but what can we do? If he could understand us, then perhaps we might come to some agreement with him. But as things are –”

“It must go,” cried the sister. “That is the only answer, Father. You simply have to stop thinking that it is Gregor. That we believed it so long – there lies our real misfortune. If this were Gregor, he would long ago have understood that human beings cannot live alongside such a beast, and he would have left of his own accord. Then we would have no brother, but we could go on living and keep his memory in honour. As it is, this creature hounds us, drives off the lodgers, and plainly means to have the flat to itself.”

Frightening anyone, his sister least of all, was the furthest thing from Gregor’s mind. He had merely started, slowly and laboriously, to turn round and head back to his room. Everyone watched him in sorrowful silence; no one urged him on. How far it was to his room! Only in the doorway did he look round – not all the way, for he felt his neck growing stiff – and he saw that behind him nothing had changed, except that his sister had risen to her feet. His last glance fell on his mother, by now sound asleep.
The moment he was over the threshold, the door was hastily pushed to, bolted and locked. “At last!” his sister cried to her parents, turning the key.

“And now?” Gregor wondered, gazing about him in the darkness. It soon dawned on him that he could not stir at all any more. That did not surprise him. The pains throughout his body seemed to be fading by degrees. The apple rotting in his back, the inflamed flesh round it under its fur of soft dust, he hardly felt. He thought of his family with tenderness and love. He was, if anything, even more convinced than his sister that he must vanish. Emptily, peacefully, he lay thinking until the church clock struck three. He still saw the sky begin to pale beyond the window. Then his head went down to the floor, though he had not willed it, and from his nostrils his final breath streamed out weakly.
## Spring

Early next morning the charwoman arrived, banging every door as usual. Taking his stillness for a sulk, she gave him a jab with her long broom; only when he slid from his place without the least resistance did she take notice. She whistled softly, then wrenched open the bedroom door and shouted into the darkness: “Just come and look, it’s croaked; there it lies, dead as a doornail!”

Mr and Mrs Samsa scrambled out of bed and into Gregor’s room. Grete came from the living room, completely dressed, her pale face suggesting she had not slept at all. “Dead?” asked Mrs Samsa. “I’d say so,” replied the charwoman, and shoved the body a good way sideways with the broom. Mrs Samsa made as if to stop her, but did not. “Well,” said Mr Samsa, “now we can give thanks to God.” He made the sign of the cross, and the women followed suit. “Look how thin he’d become,” said Grete. “He went so long without eating.” Indeed the body was entirely flat and dry. The charwoman flung the window open. Early as it was, the air already had a certain softness; it was, after all, the end of March.

When the three lodgers emerged, looking about in surprise for their breakfast, Mr Samsa came through the bedroom door in his livery, with wife and daughter on either arm. “Get out of my flat this minute!” he said. “What can you mean?” said the middle lodger, with a sickly smile. “Precisely what I say,” Mr Samsa answered. The lodger stood still, staring at the floor, as if inside his head things were quietly being put into a fresh order. “Then we shall go,” he said, and the three fetched hats and sticks, bowed silently and went.

The family decided to spend that day resting and going for a stroll; they had earned the rest, and they needed it badly. Seated at the table, they wrote three notes of apology to their employers. The charwoman came in, smiling, the small ostrich plume on her hat bobbing in all directions. “About how to clear away that thing next door,” she said, “you needn’t worry. It’s all seen to.” Mr Samsa raised a hand to stop her describing it, and she flounced off with a shocking slam of the door. “She’ll be dismissed tonight,” said Mr Samsa. Then he called to his wife and daughter, who stood holding each other by the window: “Come over here, then. Let the old business be, once and for all. And have a little thought for me, too.” At once the women came to him, caressed him and quickly finished their letters.

For the first time in months the three went out together, and rode the electric tram out into the open country past the edge of town. They had the car to themselves, and warm sunlight poured through it. They talked over what lay ahead, and found that, examined closely, their prospects were far from bad, for all three had good posts with a promising future. Above all, they would take a smaller, cheaper and more practical flat than the present one, which Gregor had picked out. Watching their daughter grow ever livelier, Mr and Mrs Samsa noticed almost in the same moment that despite all the cares that had made her cheeks pale, she had bloomed into a lovely young woman. Falling silent, and communicating almost unawares through glances, they reflected that soon they must look about for a decent husband for her. And it seemed to them a confirmation of their fresh dreams and their good resolve when, at the end of the ride, their daughter was the first to rise and stretch her young body.

quiz.q: How does Gregor manage to open the locked door of his room?
options: He pushes it with his front legs
He waits for the locksmith
He turns the key with his jaws
His sister opens it from outside

quiz.q: When Grete and her mother empty his room, what does Gregor cling to?
options: The picture of the lady in furs
His old school desk
